region: Atlantic coastal forest of eastern Brazil
description: Brazilian rosewood is a dark, richly figured rosewood long used for guitar backs and sides, fine furniture and veneer. It is now heavily restricted in international trade, so most woodworkers meet it as old stock or in musical instruments.

hazards.summary: A joiner who sanded musical instrument parts developed asthma from palisander (Dalbergia nigra) dust; a skin test and an inhalation challenge with the pure dust confirmed the cause, with a delayed asthmatic reaction.
Allergic skin rashes have been reported from items made of Brazilian rosewood, such as a bracelet and a wooden cross, and a quinone in the wood was proposed early on as the sensitizer.
The UK HSE lists rosewoods as a group (many species) as a reported cause of dermatitis, noting that effects can arise just from handling the wood.
The UK HSE also lists rosewoods as a group (many species) as a reported cause of respiratory disorders, without naming a specific mechanism.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses after long-term exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.

exposure_limits.note: Applies to wood dust generally; this species has no separate ACGIH value.

related_species_note: See rosewood (genus) and cocobolo. Dalbergia woods share related allergens and cross-reactions between them have been reported (Gamboa-2024). The name 'jacaranda' is also used for unrelated Jacaranda trees, and 'palisander' for several Dalbergia species.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed Brazilian rosewood (Dalbergia nigra) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Heartwood a rich chocolate to purplish brown with darker near-black spidery streaks and lighter reddish-orange zones; a narrow strip of pale yellowish sapwood on one edge. Bold, irregular 'spiderweb' figure with flowing dark lines, medium texture with open pores, an oily feel and a moderate natural sheen. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of Brazilian rosewood with dark brown heartwood marked by flowing black streaks.
notes_internal: HSE-WIS30 names 'Rosewood (many species)' without botanical names; applied here as group listing. The dermatitis papers (Fisher-1981, Dias-1992, OrtizBrugues-2016) have no abstracts; likely include patch tests, which would raise that hazard to level 1 once full text is checked. Common names caviuna and Rio palisander come from paper titles (Schulz-1962, Barroso 1947 PMID 20251914); caviuna is also used for Machaerium species. HSE 'dermatitis' typed as skin_sensitizer and 'respiratory disorders' as respiratory_irritant; HSE does not say which mechanism.
